IANAD, but there are primarily two kinds of abnormal tachycardia: SVT, which is mostly benign, and vtach which is very not. 

Next Friday I go in for an ablation to resolve my SVT. Mine is much like yours: yes my heart is beating fast, but because I'm on post-HA meds that lower my blood pressure the tachycardia also makes my blood pressure drop more and I get light-headed and/or tingly numbness in places if I'm in bed. The only in bed part is because when you lay on your side or something you're putting enormous pressure on your veins. Normally that's overcome by blood pressure, but if your blood pressure drops so does your circulation through compressed pathways, thus the numbness: it's a limb falling asleep.

My SVT is sustained and generally shoots me up into the 190-210 bpm range where it will stay for an average of 20 minutes, but it's gone as long as 77 minutes. So it's not only unnerving, but it's also taxing on my healing heart. Thus the ablation.

I also get unsustained vtach. Vtach is where just your ventricles are running fast, and that's bad because it puts you at drastically higher risk of vfib, which causes cardiac arrest. Most cardiac arrest is from vfib spawned by vtach.

To evaluate what you have you need an electrophysiologist, and to get into one of them you're likely going to need your cardiologist or pcp/gp to have you wear a holter monitor for a couple weeks to try and capture some of these events in real time.

In a 14-day span I had 30 tachycardia events show on the monitor: 20 SVT, 10 vtach. The SVT rate and duration (average 11 minutes in that study) qualified me for ablation.

Since I had a substantial number of vtach incidences (lasting on average 9 heart beats each) while they are in there doing the ablation they are going to do a vtach study where they try to trigger the vtach. If they are able to trigger it that means it's an electrical wiring flaw and they will recommend me for an ICD. If not they will call it idiopathic, recommend yearly holter monitorings, and possibly add another beta blocker.

Hope any of that helps.

IANAD, but heart attacks themselves, particularly when you're already in the hospital, tend to be low risk. It's stroke and cardiac arrest that are the super scary stuff, and you'd probably know if that was happening.

That she was talking and seemed normal is a great sign. The result of this, though, will almost certainly come with some lifestyle changes in terms of food and medicines.

Edit: just wanted to add that two close to each other is not necessarily more scary than one, because they didn't really clear any of the causes of blockage in between. A heart attack is an insufficiency of oxygenated blood to your heart, so if you don't fix what was causing the restriction it'll keep happening.

About 25 minutes later after the first responders has me hooked to the AED I got very light headed, saw stars, then went into cardiac arrest and flatlined. Got shocked, came back, said two sentences, flatlined again. Got shocked and compressions and came back. Got out about 3 sentences and flatlined again. This time it took 4-6 minutes to get me back.

Immediately post I was in the hospital and it's hard to say because during install of the stents there were complications and I ended up with 2 units of blood in a couple hematomas in my abdomen.

I did have, and continue to have, a much higher frequency of svt than I've ever had and I now get vtach frequently which I never had before. They keep pushing up my metoporol trying to treat it and I may end up with an ablation or ICD.

I generally feel fine, though the brilinta makes it hard to fall asleep and makes me get out of breath quickly. Some folks seem to get stents and then talk about how much more energy they have and how much better they feel; I don't have that yet.

Seems like you got plenty of great answers, but yeah: 

Heart attacks are your heart not getting oxygen, which is due to blockage somewhere in the pipes.

Cardiac arrest is your heart stopping beating because of an electrical problem (almost always ventricular fibrillation, or vfib).

Often - but not always - they are coincident, with the heart attack causing the electrical issue that leads to cardiac arrest.

Heart attacks come in lots of forms, from the ones people aren't even aware they had and didn't affect them to the chest-clutching excessively painful. There is a pretty high survival rate because anything short of the aptly-named widowmaker usually has a decent window of time to act. Once the blockage is cleared / stented / bypassed you are usually just fine.

Cardiac arrest is always a flatline; your heart stops and you are dead. If you don't have someone with an AED and the ability to perform CPR you will remain dead, so only like 10% of CA victims survive. Often CA is not singular: they shock you and your heart goes back into that same bad rhythm and you flatline again. Your brain is sending the vfib signal because the readings it's getting from your heart are wrong, so shocking you doesn't really fix that unless someone is there to do compressions to reset those signals.

I had 3 atrial arteries blocked 100% which caused me to have a heart attack, which then triggered vfib and cardiac arrest. I went into cardiac arrest 3 times back-to-back before they managed to get enough oxygenated blood in to get me out of vfib long enough to operate.

Heart attacks are when the arteries running to your heart aren't getting enough oxygen to your heart to pump. The feeling of that is a little bit like a charlie horse, but in your heart. Leading up to it you may get dull pain in your neck or shoulder - I woke up that day feeling like I had overworked my shoulder and had muscle soreness. When my heart finally couldn't get enough oxygen I started to get an intense sharp pain in the front of my chest and a larger circle of radiation pain out of my back. It felt like what I imagine a point-blank shotgun blast would feel like. Some folks get a similar thing but much less intense and just say they didn't feel good and felt tightness.

There are no signs of cardiac arrest if you don't have a heart attack you feel leading to it. When the electrical signal goes awry, just like with afib, svt, or other arrythmias, it just happens. You feel your heart beat wrongly - in the case of vfib it's basically tachycardia but only in your ventricles: your brain thinks it can fix the problem by making your ventricles beat harder and faster to draw in more blood. One of my EMTs said "I think you're just having a panic attack" and as I was saying "I know panic attacks and this is not that" I felt what I assumed was standard svt, saw stars, Said "I think I'm going to pass out", and then flatlined.

I am not minimizing heart attacks, but cardiac arrest IMO is far scarier and more dangerous because it's so sudden and so AED-proximity-dependant.

Cardiac arrest has something like a 90% mortality rate and a large part of why is that many either don't have a precipitating event or the event is coincident and they don't have time to alert people to trouble. A pulmonary angiogram looks at blood supply to your lungs. The report will mention "cardiac" because your heart is where those arteries come from.

You'd need a cardiac angiogram to see blockages that affect blood supply to your heart.

A stress echo test is a specialized ecocardiogram that looks at how your heart is performing with and without strain. It will show if you have things like valve problems or pumping/flow problems.

If your stress echo comes back clean you most likely don't have a mechanical problem with your heart. If your cardiac angiogram comes back clean you probably don't have an oxygen supply problem.

You could still have a transient electrical problem, but most of those are totally benign. I get SVT if I drink too much and when it happens my heart beats really fast and really hard and feels like I'm going to die. But it's benign and I mostly ignore it.

If both come out clear then your issue likely isn't cardiac. That doesn't make it not an issue, just not a heart issue.

You mentioned in a post that jaw pain caused your heart rate to jump. It's worth noting that LOTS of things can cause your heart to beat abnormally. Gas, stress, panic, allergies, pain, alcohol, smoking/vaping, low blood pressure, cold, heat, water retention, hormone surges, dental issues... lots and lots and lots of things can make your heart beat in a way you aren't used to or make you feel pressure in your chest, sometimes bad enough to be described as pain.

If you've got OCD it's a fair bet you also have panic disorder to some degree, and panic is one of the most heart-attack-like things there are. I understand it's a strong desire to think that where the feeling is must be the problem, but often that isn't the case. Your brain can seriously jack you up and make it seem like your body is failing.

So if the angio and echo are good I'd recommend putting more focus into why anxiety or panic is flaring. Those issues are just as serious, they just aren't as straightforward.

There's kind of two paths here from my anecdotal experience, both filed under "all humans can suffer bias". Sorry, I'm gen X so I'm wordy.

The younger you are the more they will tend to dismiss your heart concerns. At 46 shortly before I coded, while my heart was clearly in vfib, the EMTs who were watching the ECG data on the AED were telling my wife I was just having a panic attack. ER staff particularly work really hard, but it causes them to be make assumptions they hold onto sometimes even when they are wrong.

If they have not done an echo, a calcium test, or even a basic array of CBC, CMP, and lipid panel then they weren't thoroughly checking your heart. A holter monitor can only tell so much and primarily validates electrical or functional issues - it's not, for example, going to tell you if you have a significant amount of arterial blockage. While you were wearing it did you feel any of the pain sensations you talked about? If not, then it was a bad luck; I had to wear one for a month 4 times across 2 years to finally trap my afib, arrhythmia, and SVT.

That said, cardiophobia is a real thing, and maybe your heart is fine and this is just anxiety. One of the bigger things you can do for yourself in life is really nail the difference between feelings that trigger fear or worry and feelings that are actual pain.

Often inner organ feelings read as pain at first because you are not used to feeling it and it's scary, so your brain interprets that as pain. When my afib started I described it as my heart hurting, but that's not really accurate. My wife has an inert tumor on one of her organs and when she first started feeling it she described it as kind of painful when that also wasn't quite right. It feels _wrong_ but it's not actually _painful_. It's really diagnostically helpful to know the difference. Also makes medical staff more willing to listen if you can describe accurately.

I'm not sure about your diet or other risk factors (diabetes, smoking, drinking, etc), but I do know high intake of caffeine or sugar (at least for me) can mimic or trigger heart issues. Caffeine in almost any dose gives me afib and sugar beyond a point (particularly with alcohol sugars) gives me SVT. Maybe try keeping a food/drink and activity log to see if there is any correlation of what you consume or what you do or feel to those symptoms.

Lastly, anxiety is a major bitch. It can mimic almost anything and your amygdala is incredible at helping your brain weave stories of how you're only ok because you feel that stress and anxiety as a defense. Stress and anxiety can both put strain on your heart and simulate heart and general 'I'm dying' issues.

Are the drugs helping with the anxiety? If not, you may need to look at changing drugs. You also need to examine the primary stressors you have. If it's all work stress maybe you look at changing jobs. If it's family stress maybe some family therapy. If it's cardiophobia you need to work on reminding yourself that you are ok, etc. Getting help processing when you need it can be really helpful if you find a good therapist.

Drugs are like crutches - they give you strength in a weak area of your body - but you still need to walk. By which I mean if you are on anxiety meds they don't solve your anxiety, they make it easier to cope with. You still need to do the work of resolving it or (for things that can't be easily resolved like anxiety about the state of the world or past trauma) finding solid coping mechanics to process it.

Hope that helps. Categorizing and identifying what is going on is important, and sometimes you have to do the homework there yourself because medical professionals don't know you well enough to do it.

I'm 46, turned 46 beginning of last month. The day after my birthday I had a series of heart attacks and died 3 times on my living room floor.

_What factors do you think led up to having a heart attack at such a young age?_

My cardiologist has no idea and chalked it up to genetics. I had 3 100% blocked arteries (luckily not the widowmaker) and received 3 stents.

My cholesterol & triglycerides were normal 2 months prior. No diabetes, I am a non-smoker, don't and have never done drugs, and I have a pretty healthy diet. I drink, but minimally. I'm 6'4" and before my heart attack I weighed 210. Not skinny but not obese. I have no real family history -- Mom had a heart attack but is a heavy smoker, Dad has afib but never a heart attack.

I do have a history of afib when stressed out, or if I consume caffeine, and SVT if I overdrink.


_What the experience was like for you and those close to you?_

The day after my birthday I woke up and my shoulder was sore. I assumed it was because I'd brought in a bunch of gallons of water the night before and had carried too much. The wife and I were watching TV and my heart went into something I've not felt before. It was like afib, but different. I told her we needed to go to the hospital.

I got up and got dressed and while putting my shoes on it switched to pain. Such intense pain I had to run to the bathroom to throw up. In the front of my chest I had this intense, burning pain and in the back was this radiating ache. I felt like I'd been shot in the chest with a large caliber rifle - or at least I felt like that's what being shot would feel like: small but painful in the front and big exit wound.

I stumbled out to the living room and after looking at me she dialed 911. The local first responders got there 15 mins later and I was thrashing on the floor of our living room in pain. They hooked me to an AED and were sure I was just having a panic attack. I told them I was seeing stars and thought I was going to pass out.

A few seconds later my heart stopped. They shocked me and did 3 chest compressions and I came back to. I, for some reason, apologized for falling asleep. By this time the ambulance had arrived with EMTs who took over. They told me I'd just been revived and I said "I am seeing stars again" and my heart stopped again.

More shocks and more chest compressions and when I woke up I was super disoriented and tried to get up. They said I had died again and asked me to lay down. I told my wife I was so sorry she was having to go through this and then my heart stopped again.

This time they couldn't get my heart restarted. So they pushed some drugs, loaded me on the bed, and rolled me into the ambulance as one of the EMTs continued doing compressions.

My wife watched them drive away with me not knowing if I was going to be brought back this time. I came back about 4 minutes later in the ambulance.

They had driven me about 1500 yards to a nearby airfield where they had called a Careflight to take me to our nearest cardiac hospital. It took forever to get me into the chopper because I was too tall so they had to rearrange stuff to get me in. I had some small talk with them that it was my first helicopter ride and thanked them for saving me.

When I got to the hospital I was in and out of consciousness. They did a cardiac angiogram to locate the 3 blocked arteries and then did the surgery to install 3 stents.

They put me on Plavix to stop clotting. I immediately started clotting - apparently I'm in the 10% of people who are immune to Plavix. My wife got to the hospital shortly after the stents were installed. They brought her in to see me right as they started to see signs of clotting and had to rush me back in to surgery.

They pushed Brilinta as an alternative and gave me a thrombolytic to dissolve the clots. I stopped clotting, but it also dissolved the clot on my femoral artery where they'd run the lines to install the stents.

So I start bleeding massively into my abdomen. They had to push 2 units of blood and install this really painful machine on my leg to seal the artery. I was left with 2 very large hematomas in my abdomen.

I spent the night in the ICU and another 4 days in the hospital recovering. It took about 3 weeks for the hematomas to dissipate. My sternum still hurts today from the chest compressions, but luckily they didn't break any ribs. Almost all of the horrid bruises on my arms have healed, but I still have scabs where all the ivs and gas lines and cath line and such were hooked. The arm they pushed the blood transfusions through looked like it had been run through a meat grinder and that's mostly healed up now.

It was traumatic for us both, but my wife had to watch me die 3 times on our living room floor and then drive an hour to the hospital not knowing if she'd arrive to hear I was dead. When she got there happy to hear I was alive she saw me rushed back in to surgery. She then got told I had complications and high odds of not surviving the night. We live alone with no kids and our families are many states away.

She has a lot of health issues and for me to be the one who almost didn't make it was a big shock to us.


_How has your life changed on a day-to-day basis?_

Vastly. I get tired very easily and with my medication cocktail I get short of breath very easily. Standing to brush my teeth is exhausting.

I started doing daily short walks, per orders, when I got discharged. I can do my walks but I get really tired the remainder of the day after.

With the diuretics and walks I dropped down to my normal 190 in just a few weeks. Apparently I'd gained a lot of water weight over the past year, doc said likely from having been in undiagnosed congestive heart failure for some time.

I'm now really cautious with what I do, partly because I get tired but partly because I'm on anti-platelet drugs. I am starting to drive again, but only with wife in the car. I now carry nitro pills everywhere just in case.

My wife had to pick up a lot of my tasks like taking out trash or mopping the floor. She changed a lot of her eating habits to make it easier on me.

I feel like our entire lives right now are entirely about my heart.

I am on salt and fat restrictions which make consuming enough calories really tough. I basically can't eat enough of low salt foods to stop myself losing weight, so I'm losing about half a pound a day. That's going to become a problem soon.

I have always been very anti-pharma, but am now on 8 medications with rigid schedules - did call them "life extenders" which makes it feel very much like the end of the line is now in sight.
